title: Craftsmen and builders
hook: Ramgarhia Sikhs, heirs of builders and carpenters

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mazhabi Sikhs, heirs of Bhai Jaita, honored in their regiments. Your line was the guru's own sons. Who did you notice yesterday that usually goes unnoticed? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-two.

Run a hand along the doorframe of the room you're in. Somebody measured that. Somebody cut it, checked it with a level, and fixed it in place, and it's easy to go a lifetime without a thought for them. So much of what holds us up is like that: beams, stairs, window frames, the bench outside the gurdwara where the old men sit. Sikhs have a community whose name is tied to exactly this kind of work. In some cities you'll pass a gurdwara with a sign that says Ramgarhia. That name has a story behind it, and a trade.
screen: `A DOORFRAME SOMEONE MEASURED.` → `WHAT HOLDS US UP GOES UNSEEN.` → `A SIGN THAT SAYS RAMGARHIA.`

segments.voice: Start with the people. Ramgarhia Sikhs are a community who trace their families to carpenters, masons, smiths and builders. Year three told how their name came from the Ramgarhia misl, one of the old bands of Sikh riders, and from its leader, Jassa Singh, called Ramgarhia after the fort he held. So the name remembers a fort. The trade remembers something older: hands that know wood and stone. Now the oldest piece. The janamsakhis, the stories of Guru Nanak's life, tell of a carpenter named Lalo. In the story, the Guru stays in Lalo's simple home and eats his plain bread, and turns down a feast from a rich official whose wealth came from squeezing others. The bread earned by a chisel, the story says, was the honest food. It's a story, told in the old collections. But Lalo isn't only a story. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak speaks a hymn to Lalo by name, during the violence of an invasion, telling him plainly what he has seen. Third, what he tells Lalo in that hymn, here in paraphrase: as the word of the Master comes to me, so I speak it, Lalo. A hymn about where the Guru's words come from is spoken to a carpenter. Sikhs call honest work kirat. Building a wall straight is kirat. Fixing a hinge properly when nobody will check is kirat. And last, what this looks like now. When Sikh families settled in new countries, some remember builders among them raising gurdwaras with their own hands. Every one of those doors was measured by somebody.
screen: `A NAME FROM A FORT, A TRADE FROM THE HANDS.` · `LALO THE CARPENTER, AND HIS BREAD.` · `AS THE WORD COMES, SO I SPEAK, LALO.` · `GURDWARAS RAISED BY BUILDERS.` · then, large: `BUILDERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a builder. Settle, and breathe. Look around the room, slowly, and find one thing somebody made: a shelf, a stair, a window, a chair. Rest your eyes on it. Think of the person you'll never meet who cut it and fitted it. Then think of someone you do know who works with their hands: a plumber, an electrician, a cousin who fixes things, a parent who built something once. Hold their name for a breath or two, and let a plain thank-you take shape. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Craftsmen and builders. Ramgarhia Sikhs, who trace their families to carpenters, masons and smiths, and keep a name from the Ramgarhia misl. Today's word.

Your line: builders. Today, find out who built or fixed one thing you use every day, a step, a shelf, a gate, and if you can reach them, thank them and name the thing. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Ramgarhia Sikhs keep the name of the Ramgarhia misl and a memory of craft; in some cities they have their own gurdwaras, open to every Sikh, and Sikhs everywhere tell the story of Guru Nanak and Lalo the carpenter.

original.note: Punjabi: work, honest labor. kirat karni, earning by honest work, is one of the Sikh pillars.
